tecnicas.observacao: Proposta do estudo: encadeia a colaboração de três agentes (Analyst, Coder, Tester; até 3 iterações) e, se o código não passar nos testes visíveis, a depuração em tempo de execução adaptada do LDB (debugger agent + coder agent; até 4 ciclos). mecanismos_acrescentados calculados em relação ao ACT, do qual a cadeia deriva: o estágio Debugger acrescenta a explicação diagnóstica do debugger agent (raciocinio); o retorno por execução em tempo de execução cai na mesma categoria feedback já presente no laço do Tester, e multiagente/instrucao já estão no ACT. Em relação ao Debugger isolado, acrescenta decomposicao (Analyst). O contrafactual é de pacote: contra Basic (Tabela I, mesmos 19 modelos e benchmarks); os contrastes contra ACT e contra Debugger retiram um estágio inteiro, cada um com vários ingredientes e orçamento de iterações diferente, e não isolam um único mecanismo. A decomposição em blocos por CFG e o rastreamento de variáveis são instrumentação de análise/execução que alimenta o retorno (feedback); não são componentes de prompting em si.

citacoes.trecho: To enhance the LLM’s code generation abilities, we investigate, in this paper, the combination of two complementary inference-time strategies: multi-agent collaboration and runtime execution-based debugging.
In particlular, on HumanEval benchmark, across 19 LLMs, our approach achieves 64.82% accuracy compared to 56.48% achieved by the basic one-shot prompting approach.
It also outperforms the individual multi-agent collaboration approach by more than 7.66%.
Within this stage, the Analyst Agent decomposes programming tasks into smaller, manageable components and formulates a comprehensive implementation strategy.

Following this strategic outline, the Coder Agent generates the solution, progressively improving the code through an iterative process informed by the Tester Agent’s evaluation, which includes code inspection, syntactic verification, and requirements validation.
To balance computational cost and effectiveness, this refinement cycle is limited to a maximum of three iterations (retriesCT=3).
A debugger agent receives this execution trace to analyze the errors and produce diagnostic explanations, which subsequently inform a coder agent that generates revised code.
We limit this iterative debugging process to 4 cycles (retriesD = 4), a reduction from LDB’s standard 10 iterations, to balance effectiveness with computational efficiency.

We begin by segmenting the HumanEval and HumanEval+ benchmark datasets into three components: task descriptions (function identifier and natural language requirement), visible test cases (for framework execution), and hidden test cases (for final evaluation).
All models were prompted with identical role-specific instructions to ensure experimental consistency.
For decoding, we set the temperature to 0, following common practice in code generation benchmarks, as this yields deterministic output and allows for fair comparison across models.

Baseline Approaches: To evaluate our ACT + Debugger combination, we compare against five approaches: (1) Basic: Direct LLM prompting without refinement, (2) AC: Analyst-Coder collaboration with single interaction, (3) ACT: Analyst-Coder-Tester three-agent collaboration with up to 3 iterations, (4) Debugger Only: Runtime debugging without prior ACT collaboration, and (5) AC + Debugger: Analyst-Coder two-agent collaboration followed by debugging.
AC and ACT showed substantial robustness drops (129.27 and 118.51), showing that agentic interaction introduces fragility.
ACT + Debugger, despite highest accuracy, showed largest robustness drop (137.74), suggesting compounded complexity reduces code resilience.

When implementing the complete ACT + Debug chain, the results demonstrate diminishing returns, as it demands the most extensive execution time (68.42 minutes) while achieving marginally reduced accuracy (61.195%).
When debugging significantly outperforms agentic approaches, combining them introduces unnecessary complexity.
